title: On-call and Incident Response Playbook
author: Michael Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook documents Redwood Inference's standard on-call and incident response processes, runbook patterns, postmortem expectations, rotation policies, game day guidance, and status page / customer communications templates. It is intended to be the canonical source for responders and leaders during operational events.

Scope
Applies to all production-facing services maintained by Engineering, Platform, Serving Runtime, and SRE. Private deployments and customer-managed runtimes should follow the equivalent guidance in eng-private-deployments/*.

Key goals
- Minimize customer-facing impact and restore service quickly and safely.
- Maintain blameless, evidence-based postmortems that identify action items.
- Keep stakeholders informed with clear, consistent communications.
- Improve reliability through regular game days and targeted remediation.

Roles & Responsibilities
- Primary On-call (Pager): First responder for alerts during rotation window. Executes runbook steps and escalates when necessary.
- Secondary On-call (Backup): Available to assist or take over if Primary is overloaded; triages follow-ups for long incidents.
- Incident Commander (IC): If incident severity meets escalation threshold (see Severity Levels), IC coordinates cross-team work, communications, and post-incident actions. Usually a senior SRE/Platform engineer.
- Service Owner: Maintains runbooks, SLOs, and post-incident follow-ups; ensures action items are tracked.
- Communications Lead: Drafts public status updates and customer comms. Typically on-call or support lead.

Severity Levels and SLOs
- Sev 1 (Critical): Major outage, widespread customer impact, or breach of 99.9% availability SLO for > 5 minutes. Pager notification: page + phone. IC required.
- Sev 2 (High): Significant degradation impacting many customers or a major feature; potential SLO impact. Pager notification: page. IC optional based on impact.
- Sev 3 (Medium): Isolated degradation or non-critical feature issues. Alert to ticketing queue; on-call notification via chat.
- Sev 4 (Low): Informational; monitored without action unless escalated.

SLO examples (service-level, owned by service teams)
- Inference API: 99.9% availability monthly (p99 request latency < 500ms).
- Embeddings API: 99.95% availability monthly (p99 request latency < 700ms).
- Control Plane API: 99.95% availability monthly.

Alerting & Escalation Matrix
- Alerts must include: metric/threshold, runbook link, playbook ID, and next escalation step.
- Example thresholds:
  - inference-api-error-rate > 1% over 5m -> Sev 2 alert (chat + page)
  - inference-api-5xx-rate > 0.5% over 1m and request volume > 10rps -> Sev 1 page + phone
  - gpu-node-disk > 85% -> Sev 3 ticket

Escalation path (minutes to escalate):
1. Primary on-call (0–5m): acknowledge and start triage.
2. Secondary (5–15m): assist if unresolved or primary needs relief.
3. Team lead / Service owner (15–30m): engage if cross-service coordination required.
4. IC (30m+ or immediately for Sev1): appoint IC and kick off incident run.

Incident Triage Checklist (first 15 minutes)
1. Acknowledge the page. Record initial timestamp.
2. Capture scope: which services, regions, tenants affected.
3. Check dashboards (latency, error rate, capacity), logs, and recent deploys.
4. Run quick mitigation steps from runbook (e.g., failover, scale-up, rollback).
5. Post an initial incident ticket and short status update to #incidents channel.
6. If severity qualifies, notify PagerDuty rotation for IC and schedule bridge.

Runbook Pattern & Examples
- Runbooks must be owned by service teams and follow this template:
  - Title, service, owner, last_updated
  - Symptoms/alerts that trigger this runbook
  - Quick escalation criteria and severity mapping
  - Diagnostic commands (safe, read-only first)
  - Containment steps (automated or manual)
  - Recovery/restore steps
  - Post-incident remediation and links to dashboards/logs

Example: Inference API High Error Rate Runbook\Symptom:
- metric: inference-api-5xx-rate > 0.5% and increased latency (p95 > 750ms)
Immediate diagnostics (do not change production state):
- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://api.redwood.example/health
- kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide --selector=app=inference
- kubectl -n inference logs --tail=200 deployment/inference-main | grep ERROR | tail -n 50
- Check recent deploys: git log --since=\"2 hours\" --oneline deploys/inference
Containment steps (if safe):
- Scale replica pool: kubectl -n inference scale deployment/inference-main --replicas=8
- Toggle circuit-breaker: curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/feature-toggle/inference-circuitback -d '{"enabled":true}'
- Warm new nodes with cached models (automation trigger): /opt/scripts/warm_cache.sh
Recovery steps:
- If error rate drops below threshold for 10m, gradually roll back scaling or toggles.
- If recent deploy suspected, rollback to previous stable revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/inference-main
Post-incident:
- Attach relevant logs, timeline, and metrics to the incident ticket.

Incident Command (IC) Playbook
IC responsibilities:
- Own the incident timeline and declare incident severity.
- Ensure a communication cadence (initial, 15m, 30m, 1h, hourly thereafter).
- Track actions on a shared incident board (Jira/Confluence incident page).
- Decide when to escalate or engage execs.
- Lead the postmortem process and ensure action ownership.

IC checklist:
1. Confirm incident title, severity, and affected customers.
2. Create incident Confluence page and link runbooks/logs/dashboards.
3. Stand-up a bridge (Zoom/Google Meet); invite Service Owners and Product if customer-risking.
4. Author public status update and pin to #incidents for approval.
5. Assign scribe to document timeline and decisions.
6. After mitigation, mark incident as contained and start RCA work.

Communication Templates (use plain text in Slack and status page)
- Initial Slack / Incident Channel template (15–30 lines):
  [INCIDENT] [Sev {level}] {short-title} — {1-line summary}
  Impact: {who/what is affected}
  Start time: {HH:MM UTC}
  Scope: {regions/services/tenants}
  Mitigation in progress: {brief bullet}
  IC: {name} | Primary responder: {name}
  Next update: {time}

- Public status page templates
  - Major outage (Sev1):
    Title: Major outage affecting Inference API (All regions)
    Summary: We are currently experiencing an outage impacting text generation and embeddings across all regions. Our engineers are actively investigating.
    Impact: API requests are failing or timing out.
    Latest update: {timestamp} — {short update}
    Next update: {ETA or cadence}
  - Partial degradation (Sev2):
    Title: Partial degradation for embeddings API in us-west-2
    Summary: Customers in us-west-2 may see elevated latency and increased error rates. Mitigation steps underway.

- Customer-facing email template (for incidents impacting SLAs)
  Subject: Incident report — {service} degraded on {date} (ID: {incident-id})
  Body:
  Hello {CustomerName},

  We are contacting you to inform you about an incident that affected {service} on {date}. Summary: {one-line summary}. Impact: {who was affected and approximate duration}. Current status: {resolved / under mitigation}. Next steps: {what we will do to prevent recurrence}. For a detailed timeline and root cause analysis, we will follow up with a post-incident report within 3 business days.

  Regards,
  Redwood Inference Support

Postmortem Expectations
- Postmortem must be created within 72 hours of incident containment.
- Template fields:
  - Title, incident ID, severity, owners, timeline, root cause, contributing factors, detection and response timeline, customer impact, action items (with owners and due dates), follow-ups, and link to dashboards/logs.
- Postmortems are blameless, focus on systemic fixes, and must include measurable remediation (test coverage, automation, config changes, runbook updates).
- Action items should be tracked in Jira and closed within agreed timeframes (critical: 14 days, high: 30 days, medium: 90 days).

On-call Rotation Policy
- Rotation cadence: 1-week rotations for Platform and SRE on-call; 2-week rotations for smaller service teams where appropriate.
- Shift coverage: primary on-call covers weekdays and weekends; secondary is on-call 24/7 for escalation.
- Handover procedure: outgoing on-call must publish a handoff note in #oncall-handoffs including active incidents, unstable services, and outstanding action items.
- Time off and backup: request time-off in the on-call calendar and arrange a swap at least 72 hours in advance. For unexpected absences, notify the on-call manager and allocate a temporary backup.
- Burnout policy: teams must monitor on-call load; individuals with 3+ high-severity incidents in a rotation are eligible for a recovery day.

Game Days & Reliability Exercises
- Purpose: validate runbooks, test failover procedures, and surface systemic weaknesses in a controlled environment.
- Cadence: Quarterly cross-team game days (SRE + Platform + Serving Runtime) + targeted monthly team-level drills.
- Typical scenarios:
  - Region failover (simulate network partition).
  - Model loading cold-start and cache warm-up failure.
  - Control plane database latency spike.
  - Gradual resource exhaustion (CPU/GPU/IO).
- Game day deliverables:
  - Post-exercise report with timeline, what worked, gaps found, and prioritized remediation plan.
  - Update runbooks and automation within 2 weeks for critical gaps.

Status Page and External Communications
- Status page ownership: Customer Success + Communications Lead + Service Owner.
- Severity mapping for status page entries:
  - Major outage (Sev1): public status + email to affected customers (if SLA-impacting).
  - Degradation (Sev2): public status entry; targeted emails for affected customers.
  - Maintenance (planned): scheduled update 48h prior.
- Message cadence: initial, every 30 minutes for Sev1 until contained, then hourly until resolved.

Templates for Status Page entries (short form)
- Title: {short description}
- Affected services: {list}
- Impact: {what customers see}
- Latest update: {time + short message}
- Next update: {ETA}
- Root cause (post-incident): {summary}

Training, Metrics, and Continuous Improvement
- Key incident metrics tracked monthly:
  - Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA)
  - Mean Time to Restore (MTTR)
  - Number of Sev1/Sev2 incidents per quarter
  - % of postmortem action items completed on time
- Training: new on-call engineers must shadow for one rotation and complete the on-call checklist.
- Weekly reliability review: SRE + Platform lead reviews recent incidents and progress on action items.

Appendices
A. Incident Checklist (one-page printable)
- Acknowledge -> Triage -> Contain -> Communicate -> IC -> Resolve -> Postmortem
\B. Quick Commands (examples)
- kubectl -n inference get pods
- kubectl -n inference logs deployment/inference-main --since=10m
- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.redwood.example/health
\C. Postmortem Template (copy/paste)
- Title: {Incident title}
- Incident ID: {ID}
- Severity: {Sev}
- Start/End times: {UTC}
- Summary: {one-paragraph}
- Timeline: {minute-by-minute}
- Root cause: {summary}
- Contributing factors: {list}
- Detection & response: {what alerted, who acted}
- Impact: {customer-facing impact}
- Action items: {owner | due date | status}
- Follow-ups: {links to dashboards/logs}

D. Contacts & Escalation Directory
- PagerDuty: rotation schedules are maintained in PagerDuty (link: https://pagerduty.example/teams/redwood).
- Exec escalation: ops-contacts@redwood.example (on-call manager will notify).

Ownership and Review Cycle
- Document owner: Platform Reliability (team).
- Review cadence: annual formal review, or after any Sev1 incident.

Related pages

- Runbook repository: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks
